section_summary: This section covers diplomatic, political, and ideological developments concerning Japan during World War II between early and mid-1942, as recorded in U.S. State Department records. It includes an extensive American diplomatic report reviewing Japanese foreign relations across Southeast Asia, the Vatican, and Latin America, alongside domestic political consolidation under the Imperial Rule Assistance Association, wartime economic measures, civilian morale, and anti-Allied propaganda. It also contains an April 1942 despatch from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew enclosing a Japanese press clipping on the duties of second-generation Japanese Americans (Nisei), and an August 1942 despatch from Consul General Harold B. Quarton transmitted aboard the repatriation ship M/S Gripsholm transmitting and analyzing Professor Chikao Fujisawa's ultra-nationalist pamphlet on Shinto mythology, imperial divinity, and Japan's global mission.

subfiles.about: A comprehensive diplomatic review detailing Japanese foreign policy, domestic political reorganization, economic controls, civilian morale, and wartime propaganda during the first six months of the Pacific War.
subfiles.summary: This report covers Japanese external relations and internal wartime conditions from late 1941 to mid-1942. In foreign affairs, it details the border delimitation agreement between Manchukuo and Outer Mongolia, the progressive subjugation of French Indo-China, the alliance and currency agreements with Thailand, the establishment of diplomatic representation at the Vatican, policies toward the occupied Philippines, and Tokyo's reaction to the Rio de Janeiro Conference. Domestically, it examines the 1942 Diet general election, the dominance of the Imperial Rule Assistance Association (IRAA) and Imperial Rule Assistance Political Association (IRAPA), national budgets, commodity rationing, civilian morale, and critical shipping bottlenecks. It concludes with an analysis of anti-Allied propaganda and atrocity allegations, the seizure of enemy assets and social clubs, revisions to the Bank of Japan Law, and policies toward ethnic Chinese merchants in Southeast Asia.
subfiles.title: Review of Japanese Foreign Relations, Domestic Politics, Economic Controls, and Wartime Propaganda

subfiles.about: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew transmits to the Secretary of State a newspaper clipping summarizing an article by Professor Takizo Matsumoto concerning the obligations of second-generation Japanese (Nisei) in Hawaii and the continental United States.
subfiles.summary: Grew forwards a clipping on Professor Matsumoto's article urging Nisei protect their parents' property and heritage, framing Japan's war as a justice campaign despite American discrimination.
subfiles.title: Transmitting Clipping Regarding Magazine Article Concerning Second Generation Japanese by Professor Takizo Matsumoto of Meiji University, Tokyo

subfiles.about: An internal State Department memorandum analyzing Consul General Harold B. Quarton's despatch and Otto Tolischus's summary of Professor Chikao Fujisawa's ultra-nationalist Shinto pamphlet.
subfiles.summary: FE calls Quarton's transmitted Fujisawa pamphlet mystical nonsense claiming mankind must submit to the Emperor, reflecting wartime Japan's decayed objective thought.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Consul General Quarton's Despatch Transmitting Pamphlet by Professor Chikao Fujisawa

subfiles.about: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew forwards Consul General Harold B. Quarton's despatch transmitting and analyzing Professor Chikao Fujisawa's ideological treatise on Shinto cosmology and Japan's global mission.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew and Harold B. Quarton
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew forwards a despatch prepared on board the repatriation vessel M/S Gripsholm by Consul General Harold B. Quarton, which transmits an English-language pamphlet by Professor Chikao Fujisawa along with a journalistic analysis by Otto Tolischus. Quarton recounts that the original pamphlet was obtained by Presbyterian missionary Dr. Edwin W. Koons while imprisoned in Keijo and was smuggled out of Korea by his wife. Fujisawa's treatise synthesizes Shinto mythology, pseudohistory, and totalitarian philosophy, arguing that Japan was the primordial cradle of mankind and that the Emperor is the absolute cosmic life-center destined to unite all nations under the divine principle of Musubi. The text interprets the Pacific War as a sacred purification ritual (O-harai) to cleanse humanity of Western individualism, capitalism, and Marxism, restoring a prehistoric universal family order.
subfiles.title: The Great Shinto Purification Ritual and the Divine Mission of Nippon, a Prophesy of the Dawn of a New Age
